# Oil cooler hose replacement

> **[Unverified]** This page rests on a single community report. Cross-check before relying on it.

> Items marked **[Partial]** are only partly confirmed by the source and need more work. They stay in the review queue and are firmed up, corrected or removed as more sources come in.

## Summary

[Partial] Replace an oil cooler hose by removing surrounding components and installing new clamps. [t759]

## Procedure

> **[Partial]** Needs more work: the verifier could confirm only part of this procedure (the steps marked [Partial], or whether the list is complete). Steps or precautions may be wrong or missing; read the source thread before relying on it. Later runs fill it in as more sources are found.

1. Remove the engine cover by taking out two 10mm bolts.
2. [Partial] Loosen the air intake clamps and remove its two 10mm bolts along with the PCV valve cover to intake hose.
3. Unbolt the bracket for the air intake using two 13 or 14mm bolts.
4. Remove the VIAS bolts to rotate them out of the way.
5. Unbolt the metal tube connecting to the target hose by removing its two bolts.
6. Detach the evap hose running over to the throttle body and remove the valve cover to valve cover PCV hose.
7. Pull the existing metal tube out from inside the old hose you are replacing.
8. Push the side of the hose against an angle while using needle nose pliers to grab and pull off the upper clamp.
9. Grab the end of the hose with regular needle nose pliers and attempt to pull it free.
10. Cut the stuck hose in half near where it connects back into the metal tube if it does not budge.
11. [Partial] Wedge a long flat tip screwdriver between the remaining lower clamp and the hose, then twist repeatedly until the clamp rotates to face you.
12. Reach down with needle nose pliers to grab the rotated clamp and pull it off completely.
13. Pull the rest of the old hose away from the engine connection point.
14. Install the new hose onto the metal tube located on the outside of the engine, ensuring its first clamp is in place.
15. Place a second clamp on the end of the new hose going into the engine about 1½ inches above the tip and orient it to face you when installed.
16. Use the outer metal tube as a guide to maneuver the new hose onto the inner metal tube inside the engine until fully seated.
17. Gently grab the newly positioned hose with needle nose pliers to help push it firmly into place without tearing it.
18. [Partial] Position and secure the second clamp over the connection point where you just pushed the hose on.

_Procedure reported by [t759]. Photos of this job are in the source: <https://www.xterranation.org/index.php?threads/how-to-change-oil-cooler-hose-coolant-return-to-engine.8851/>_

## Tools

- Crescent PSX204C X2 Long Reach Plier Set [t759]
- Long flat tip screwdriver (at least 12 inches) [t759]
- Small flashlight (two recommended) [t759]
- Magnetic pickup tool [t759]
- Metric socket set starting at 10mm with a short extension [t759]

## Parts

- Nissan Hose Part# 21306-EA200: Listed as part #21308 on diagrams; coolant return to engine. [t759]
- Valve Cover to Intake Hose (# 11826-ZL80B): Recommended replacement during this job if the original cracks. [t759]
- [Partial] Valve Cover to Valve Cover Hose, PCV (# 11826-EA200): Recommended for older trucks as it tends to crack. [t759]

## Tips & gotchas

- Use a magnetic pickup tool in case you drop small parts into tight spaces. [t759]
- [Partial] Switch between different pliers to get leverage on the hose clamps. [t759]
- Cut the old hose in half close to the metal tube if it resists pulling out, using a razor blade at the end of your pliers. [t759]

## Common mistakes

- [Partial] Forgetting that older trucks often have cracked PCV hoses which can lead to leaks later. [t759]
